METHODOLOGY. This family treats BTC's price, in the limit of zero discounted-cashflow fundamental, as a rational bubble in the Blanchard (1979) / Blanchard-Watson (1982) / Tirole (1985 Econometrica) tradition, ported to crypto by van Oordt (2024), Biais et al. (JoF 2023), and bounded below by Schilling-Uhlig (JME 2019). The load-bearing result is a no-arbitrage IDENTITY: in equilibrium the expected return on a price that contains a rational bubble component must EQUAL the ordinary required return on risk capital - 'as is the case for all other financial assets' (van Oordt, verbatim). The intuition van Oordt spells out is the standard rebuttal to the 'BTC will outgrow all wealth' critique: if a single asset's bubble earned above the common required return, its share of total wealth would grow without bound in expectation, which cannot be an equilibrium; if below, no one holds it. Hence E[r] = required return, full stop. With a Blanchard-Watson stochastic structure, the price 'grows at a faster speed than the required return as long as the bubble persists, but there is a positive probability the bubble will burst. The expected return on such a stochastic bubble path still equals the required return because the higher rate of appreciation is counterbalanced by the downside risk' (van Oordt, verbatim). That is the explicit 'required return + crash hazard' decomposition: survival-conditional drift = rho + h*LGC, unconditional E[r] = rho.\n\nKEY RELATIONSHIPS. Van Oordt decomposes price into a transactional-demand FLOOR (a baseline-equilibrium path = the PV-analogue of net transactional benefits, below which negative bubbles are ruled out by an assumption) plus an additive bubble term. Sustaining the bubble requires ongoing NET INVESTMENT INFLOWS that rise with new-coin issuance and the required return and the level of transactional demand, and fall with growth in transactional demand; for non-negative money growth, bubble participants earn 'Ponzi-scheme equivalent payoffs in the aggregate' even though each individual's expected return meets their required return - a striking, honest framing. Biais et al. build the empirical counterpart: BTC fundamental value = stream of net transactional benefits (which themselves depend on future prices, a fixed point), PLUS sunspots => multiple equilibria and extrinsic volatility. Their calibration is the most useful hard output: changes in fundamentals explain only 'around 5%' of BTC return variance (so ~95% is extrinsic/sunspot); required WEEKLY BTC returns start above 10%/week early in 2011-19 and DECAY to ~2%/week by sample end; crash risk contributes ~11 percentage points of the early required return, declining thereafter, and illiquidity (difficulty exchanging BTC) adds ~10pp early dropping to ~8pp. Schilling-Uhlig provide the floor/martingale: with two intrinsically worthless currencies, the fundamental pricing equation makes the dollar BTC price a MARTINGALE (Q_t = E_t[Q_{t+1}]); BTC must 'rise in expectation and earn a real interest' ONLY if the speculative ('hodling') condition holds; under their Assumption 3 (mutual impatience) the speculative condition fails, so the fundamental pricing equation applies and BTC's expected real return equals the real rate, with fundamental value possibly zero - and the price can be a convergent supermartingale falling toward that zero. Tirole supplies the macro feasibility ceiling: a deterministic bubble grows at the gross interest rate and can persist only in a dynamically inefficient economy (r <= g); with r > g indefinite real appreciation is generically infeasible.\n\nHISTORICAL FIT & FAILURE MODES. Empirically the appeal is that the framework PREDICTS what we observe - extreme, largely non-fundamental volatility (Biais ~95% extrinsic), recurrent crashes, and a required return that decays - without needing scarcity numerology. Its honesty about the left tail (Schilling-Uhlig collapse-to-zero, Biais sunspot equilibrium shift) is a genuine strength versus single-path level models. The failure modes are real: it is positive not normative, so it yields an identity and a distribution but no unique point CMA; the required return and crash hazard are exogenous free parameters; multiplicity means the model cannot tell you WHICH equilibrium obtains; and it is silent on every cross-asset correlation (all imported from realized data). Its starkest implication - that forward EXPECTED return is just a risk-required return (~high single digits to low teens), far below realized survivor history - is exactly what makes it the rigorous backbone for the appreciation-decay haircut, and exactly why bulls dislike it.\n\nON-RECORD MULTI-YEAR FORECASTS. The academic papers deliberately publish NO dated multi-year BTC price/return forecast - that abstention is itself a stance (they hold expected return is the required return and the rest is sunspot). The only quantified on-record outputs are Biais et al.'s calibrated required-return path (>10%/week -> ~2%/week, with ~11pp early crash-risk and ~10pp early illiquidity contributions) over 2011-2019, and Schilling-Uhlig's martingale/real-rate floor. No gold-parity, S2F-style, or power-law multi-million target exists in this family - and that is precisely its disciplinary value for a 10-15yr CMA.

</details>

### #8 · Mining-Economics Dynamics & Security-Budget Sustainability (Hashprice, Hash/Difficulty Ribbons, Puell, Cost-Curve, Supply-Elasticity)

*Family: mining-economics-dynamics · Source: Practitioner · Tier: Conditioning overlay · Overall 65*


**Explanation:** This family reads Bitcoin through miner economics in MOTION rather than a static cost level. Hashprice (USD/PH/s/day) is the unit revenue miners earn — driven by subsidy, fees, difficulty, and price. When hashprice falls below high-cost miners' cash cost, the hash/difficulty ribbon and Puell Multiple flag capitulation: weak rigs switch off, difficulty drops, forced selling clears, and the market tends to bottom. The heterogeneous cost curve (low-cost survivors at the bottom) plus a ~0.7 hashrate-price elasticity (asymmetric — fast up, sticky down) loosely bound drawdowns. But the load-bearing insight is COST-ENDOGENEITY: because difficulty re-targets, security spend stays a near-constant ~1% share of transacted value, so cost FOLLOWS price — it cannot anchor it. For a 10-15yr CMA this is deflationary: there is no exogenous rising cost floor lifting price, and the declining subsidy makes the security budget depend on a fee market that does not yet exist at scale. The honest implication is a decay-extrapolated forward return, with miner stress signals useful only for cycle timing, not for the long-horizon level.


*Scores — rigor 4, signal 2, robustness 4, data-ops 4, orthogonality 4. High rigor: grounded in observable industrial data and unusually honest via the Song-Aste cost-endogeneity critique (cost follows price, so no exogenous cost-floor). But that same insight kills its level signal — none of the instruments is a return forecaster, so a 10-15yr appreciation requires bolting on exogenous price/fee assumptions; signal is weak. Robust because cost-endogeneity (~constant ~1% security spend) is regime-invariant through halvings, the S2F break, and ETF era, and capitulation signals add genuine tail/regime conditioning. Data-ops strong: hashprice, difficulty, J/TH, $/kWh are refreshable and pipeline-friendly.*


**Key drivers:** Hashprice (USD/PH/s/day) = f(block subsidy, transaction fees, network difficulty, BTC price) — the unit revenue of mined hashrate; ~$34/PH/day at 5yr lows in Feb 2026; Block-subsidy halving schedule (3.125 BTC in 2025 → 1.5625 ~2028 → ~0 by 2140) — mechanically halves the issuance-revenue leg of hashprice and the security budget every ~4yr; Network difficulty / hashrate — self-adjusts every 2016 blocks to hold ~10-min blocks; rises with miner entry (raising cost), falls on capitulation (the difficulty/hash-ribbon signal); Heterogeneous miner cost curve: electricity $/kWh × rig efficiency (J/TH); low-cost oligopoly survivors (Arnosti-Weinberg) set the marginal cost of security and bound drawdown depth; Electricity-price / hashrate elasticity ~0.69-0.71 short-run, 0.33-0.40 long-run (NBER w31745); asymmetric — hashrate ramps fast on price rises, sticks on price falls; Puell Multiple = daily USD issuance / 365d MA — miner-income oscillator (<0.5 capitulation, >3-4 euphoria); Fee-to-subsidy security-budget transition: fees ~1-5% of reward today; must grow to sustain security spend as subsidy → 0; Cost-endogeneity (Song-Aste): difficulty adjustment holds security spend ~constant (~1%) share of value transferred, so cost tracks price


**Pros:** Grounds Bitcoin in a real, observable, refreshable industrial dataset (hashprice, difficulty, J/TH efficiency, $/kWh) rather than pure price extrapolation or narrative — communicable to commodity/utility investors; The capitulation signals have genuine ex-post cyclical content: hash-ribbon crossovers and Puell <0.5 have bracketed several major bottoms (miner forced-selling exhaustion is a real, mechanical clearing event), giving a defensible cycle-timing overlay; Honest about its own limits via the cost-endogeneity critique (Song-Aste): the framework itself supplies the strongest argument AGAINST naive cost-floor bull cases — security spend is a ~constant ~1% share of value transferred, so cost can't lead price. This intellectual discipline is rare in BTC valuation; The natural-oligopoly cost-curve (Arnosti-Weinberg) gives a structural reason drawdowns have a soft floor: when price falls, only low-cost survivors remain, difficulty drops, and the marginal cost of security compresses toward the price — a real mean-reverting attractor, not a hard floor but a directional force; The ~0.7 short-run elasticity is a peer-reviewed, causally-identified estimate (NBER natural experiment), not a curve-fit — rare empirical rigor for a BTC input


**Cons:** Cost-endogeneity is fatal to any cost-as-floor CMA: difficulty re-targets so cost FOLLOWS price (causality price→cost). Song-Aste show the cost/value ratio has been ~constant (~1%) since 2010 despite a ten-billion-fold hashing increase — there is no exogenous rising cost floor to lift price over a decade; None of the instruments is a return forecaster. Hashprice, Puell, and the ribbons are unit-revenue / stress / timing signals; deriving a 10-15yr appreciation requires bolting on price and fee-growth assumptions the framework does not supply; The security-budget transition is an unresolved existential risk, not a tailwind: as subsidy → 0, fees (currently ~1-5% of reward) must replace it. If they don't, the security budget — and thus the cost anchor and possibly the network's integrity — erodes. The framework cannot tell you whether the fee market materializes; Capitulation signals have degraded post-financialization: ETF/treasury marginal buyers never touch the chain, miners are diversifying to AI/HPC (decoupling hashrate from BTC economics), and 2026 saw the first multi-year hashrate drop as miners pivoted to AI — breaking the price↔hashrate link the ribbons depend on; Silent on volatility-as-a-stat and on all cross-asset correlations (growth/value eq, FI, TIPS, gold) — every distributional CMA cell must be imported from realized data; Tiny cyclical sample (3-4 halvings) and reflexivity: market cap drives mining revenue which drives the very signals used to value the market — circular

METHODOLOGY. This family is a bundle of practitioner instruments stitched to one academic critique. Hashprice (Luxor, coined 2019) is the keystone: the expected daily USD revenue per unit of hashrate, quoted USD/PH/s/day, a deterministic function of four inputs — block subsidy, transaction fees, network difficulty, and BTC price (Luxor uses a 144-block lagging MA for fees and a 3-exchange spot average for USD). It is the unit price of the commodity miners sell. As of Feb 2026 hashprice sits at 5-year lows (~$34/PH/day) against large-miner all-in cost ~$44/PH/day — i.e., the marginal public miner is underwater, the textbook capitulation setup. The Puell Multiple (David Puell, Mar 2019) normalizes daily USD issuance by its 365-day MA into an oscillator: <0.5 = miner-revenue stress / historical bottoms, >3-4 = euphoria / tops. The Difficulty Ribbon (Willy Woo) and its derivative Hash Ribbons (Charles Edwards / Capriole, 2019) read 30- vs 60-day hashrate SMA crossovers: a downward cross marks capitulation (inefficient rigs power off, forced-sell coins, difficulty later drops ~2 weeks behind), an upward recross is the buy. These are timing/stress signals, NOT return forecasters.

KEY RELATIONSHIPS. The heterogeneous miner cost curve is the structural backbone. Arnosti & Weinberg (arXiv:1811.08572; Management Science 2022) prove Bitcoin mining is a NATURAL OLIGOPOLY: with economies of scale (return exponent α>1) every survivor holds market share ≥ 1−1/α, so the market sustains at most α/(α−1) miners, and a miner with 20%-lower costs must hold ≥20% of hashpower. This means low-cost survivors set the marginal cost of security, giving drawdowns a soft (not hard) floor. The hashrate-price ELASTICITY quantifies the dynamics: Papp, Almond & Zhang (NBER w31745 / Columbia CEEP WP27, 2023), exploiting a coal plant with on-site mining as a natural experiment, estimate short-run elasticity ~0.69-0.71 and long-run 0.33-0.40 — and the response is asymmetric (hashrate ramps quickly on price strength via rig deployment, sticks on weakness as paid-for rigs run until cash-cost-negative). They also find a $1 BTC price rise causes $3.11-6.79 of carbon damages, exceeding mining's value added — the "digital crude, not digital gold" finding that undercuts the monetary framing.

THE LOAD-BEARING CRITIQUE — COST-ENDOGENEITY. Song & Aste (arXiv:2004.04605; Frontiers in Blockchain 2020) show that despite a ~10-billion-fold rise in hashing and ~10-million-fold rise in energy use, the cost of PoW RELATIVE TO VALUE TRANSFERRED has neither risen nor fallen since 2010, staying ~1%. Their security argument: PoW must cost a sizable, roughly constant fraction of the value transferable to deter double-spends, so the difficulty adjustment endogenously holds security spend ~proportional to value. The fatal CMA implication: cost is a CONSEQUENCE of price, not a cause. There is no exogenous, rising cost floor to lift price over a decade — every cost-based bull case ("production cost is $77k so price can't fall below") inverts the causality. When price falls, miners exit, difficulty drops, and cost falls to follow.

SECURITY-BUDGET TAIL. The subsidy halves toward zero (3.125 BTC in 2025 → ~0 by 2140); fees are ~1-5% of the block reward today. For the security budget — and thus the cost anchor — to persist, a fee market must scale. The framework cannot tell you if it will; this is an unpriced left-tail, sharpened by the 2026 miner pivot to AI/HPC (first multi-year hashrate drop), which partially decouples hashrate from BTC economics and degrades the ribbon/Puell signals.

ON-RECORD MULTI-YEAR FORECASTS. This family produces almost NO clean multi-year price forecasts — by construction. Practitioners use it for cycle timing (Capriole's hash-ribbon bottom calls; Puell <0.5 bottom flags) and for current cost levels (JPMorgan's rolling production-cost series: ~$90k early-2026 → ~$77k). The one durable quantitative on-record claim is Song-Aste's: security cost ≈ 1% of value transferred, constant since 2010 — which forecasts that cost will keep tracking price, not anchoring it. HISTORICAL FIT: capitulation signals fit pre-2021 cycles well; post-financialization (ETF/treasury buyers, AI diversification) they have weakened. FAILURE MODES: causality inversion (treating an endogenous cost as a floor), reflexivity (market cap drives the mining revenue that drives the signals), tiny 3-4-halving sample, and the unresolved fee-market transition. Net: the most analytically honest of the cost-family approaches and the one that most forcefully argues for a DECAY-extrapolated, low-single-to-high-single-digit forward CMA — because its own central result says cost cannot do the bulls' work.

### #9 · Reflexive / Log-Periodic Bubble & Crash-Hazard (LPPLS / JLS)

*Family: bubble-hazard · Source: Academia · Tier: Conditioning overlay · Overall 62*


**Explanation:** This approach treats a Bitcoin bull run as an endogenous bubble rather than a trend to extrapolate. Built on the Johansen-Ledoit-Sornette rational-expectations model and its Log-Periodic Power Law Singularity (LPPLS) calibration, it casts price as faster-than-exponential ("super-exponential") growth driven by herding and positive feedback, accelerating toward a finite critical time t_c at which a time-varying crash-hazard rate peaks. Wheatley, Sornette et al. (Royal Society Open Science, 2019) anchor "fundamental value" with a generalized Metcalfe's law (market cap proportional to active-users^1.69, R^2=0.95) and flag four historical bubbles with 3.1x-103x runups followed by >50% crashes. The model outputs a probabilistic crash bracket, not a date. For a CMA it yields a distinctive shape: E[r] = super-exponential drift minus hazard times expected crash size. The decision-relevant implication is the gap between a ~12-16% nominal arithmetic drift and only ~4-9% geometric (compounded) return once recurring 50-80% endogenous drawdowns are netted out, with vol clustering near 60-70% and correlations imported from realized data.


*Scores — rigor 3, signal 2, robustness 2, data-ops 2, orthogonality 4. LPPLS/JLS has a real theoretical pedigree and a measurable network anchor (generalized Metcalfe), but its 7+ nonlinear parameters guarantee high in-sample fit regardless of a true bubble, and t_c is notoriously unstable, so its predictive signal for a 10-15yr level is weak. It is a within-cycle hazard timer, not a regime-survivor: the value it adds is fat-left-tail/crash-hazard conditioning, not the decay-anchored level the CMA already needs. No native CMA number means every horizon figure is analyst reconstruction, and recalibration across windows is operationally heavy.*


**Key drivers:** Positive-feedback / reflexive demand: herding, imitation and momentum buying that produce faster-than-exponential (super-exponential) price growth — the core JLS mechanism; Crash hazard rate h(t) rising toward a finite-time critical point t_c; expected return is drift net of hazard x expected jump size; Log-periodic oscillations (discrete scale invariance) — accelerating up/down swings interpreted as spirals of fear/greed, used as the bubble fingerprint; Generalized Metcalfe fundamental support: network value ~ active users^1.69, growing sub-quadratically; the price-to-Metcalfe (MMV) ratio gates overvaluation; Maturation / decay: as the user base and adoption S-curve flatten, the sustainable super-exponential drift decays and bubbles become smaller in relative magnitude; Endogenous instability state (monitorable) vs. exogenous trigger (unpredictable) — the model claims to time the *regime*, not the spark


**Pros:** Produces a genuinely different CMA *shape* — a hazard-weighted, fat-left-tailed return distribution — instead of a single mean/vol, which is more faithful to BTC's actual crash-prone history (four >50% drawdowns documented 2012-2018); Has a fundamental anchor (generalized Metcalfe, users^1.69, R^2~0.95) so overvaluation is measurable rather than asserted; ties price to an on-chain network observable; Ex-ante, real-time: the LPPLS confidence indicator flagged elevated instability before the 2013 and 2017 BTC peaks, giving probabilistic warning windows rather than post-hoc storytelling; Honestly separates what is forecastable (the bubble regime / hazard) from what is not (the exact crash date and trigger) — intellectually disciplined about its own limits; Captures reflexivity and momentum that mean-reverting or random-walk CMAs structurally miss; directly models the compounding penalty crashes impose on long-horizon geometric returns


**Cons:** Severe overfitting risk: the LPPLS function has 7+ nonlinear parameters and fits accelerating/oscillating data almost regardless of whether a true bubble exists — high in-sample R^2 is nearly guaranteed and not evidence; Critical-time t_c is notoriously unstable: published replications show t_c jumping by weeks depending on the initial guess and the calibration window; point predictions are effectively meaningless (authors themselves call long-term single-model predictions 'misleading'); No native, validated CMA number: the framework yields hazard windows and bubble flags, not a 10-15yr expected-return/vol figure — every quantitative CMA under it is the analyst's reconstruction, not a published output; Tiny sample of genuine bubbles (4) makes false-positive vs. miss rates statistically ambiguous; out-of-sample, real-time crash 'predictions' have a poor and contested track record; Generalized Metcalfe support is itself fragile: the 1.69 exponent is fit to one asset's short history, user/active-address counts are noisy and gameable, and price feeds back into usage, contaminating the 'fundamental'; Says nothing useful about cross-asset correlations (gold, TIPS, equities, FI) — those rows are silent in the literature, so correlation inputs must come entirely from elsewhere; Explicitly blind to exogenous shocks ('massive exogenous shocks could occur at any time, and the LPPLS model can provide no warning there') — exactly the tail an investor most cares about

(Otherwise it reads as inconsistent with the consensus.)", "In pros #3, soften 'flagged elevated instability before the 2013 and 2017 BTC peaks' to note this is the paper's claimed ex-ante performance, which cons #4 correctly flags as contested out-of-sample — so the reader sees the pro and con are abo

Core BTC reference: Wheatley, Sornette, Huber, Reppen, Gantner (Royal Society Open Science, 2019; arXiv:1803.05663). LPPLS log-price model: ln(p) = A + (t_c - t)^m [B + C cos(omega ln(t_c - t) + phi)], with 0<m<1, fitted m roughly 0.10-0.43 and log-periodic omega roughly 7.8-12 across the four BTC bubbles; AR(1) phi 0.87-0.99. Fundamental anchor is a generalized Metcalfe's law: market cap ~ active-users^1.69 (beta = 1.69 +/- 0.008, R^2 ~ 0.95 over 2010-2018), explicitly rejecting classic N^2. Four documented BTC bubbles: 2012 (3.1x runup), early-2013 (20.4x), late-2013 (6.8x), and the 2015-2017 run (~103x to ~$20k). At writing (Mar 2018, ~$170B cap) the price-to-Metcalfe ratio implied roughly 4x-8x overvaluation vs support. CMA derivation logic: E[r] = super-exponential drift - h(t) x E[crash size]; over 10-15yr the drift decays with network maturation while the hazard of 50-80% drawdowns recurs, mechanically depressing geometric vs arithmetic return and producing a fat-left-tailed, negatively skewed distribution — this is the row's distinctive contribution: it is a survival/return-process shape, not a point. Brutally honest caveats (well-documented in the literature and replications): (1) LPPLS overfits — 7+ nonlinear params fit any accelerating/oscillating series; high in-sample R^2 is not evidence of a bubble; (2) t_c is unstable — replications show the predicted critical time shifting by weeks with the initial guess/window, and the authors concede single-model long-horizon predictions are 'effectively meaningless'; (3) the model is explicitly blind to exogenous shocks ('the LPPLS model can provide no warning there'); (4) only 4 true bubbles -> false-positive vs miss rates are statistically ambiguous, and out-of-sample real-time skill is contested. Correlation cells are 'n/a (source silent)' in cited_outputs because this literature does not report cross-asset correlations at all; the synthesized correlations are imported from general BTC market data (BTC-gold ~0 long-run per NYDIG; BTC-equity ~0.2-0.4) and flagged as judgment. Numbers in synthesized_outputs are the analyst's reasoned 10-15yr judgment under this approach's hazard logic, NOT published model outputs.

### #10 · Tail-Risk Implied Required Return (CVaR / Expected-Shortfall Pricing)

*Family: tail-insurance-pricing · Source: Academia · Tier: Conditioning overlay · Overall 62*


**Explanation:** Variance treats a 30% gain and a 30% crash identically; CVaR/Expected Shortfall does not — it averages only the worst alpha% of outcomes, the left tail investors actually fear. Rockafellar-Uryasev (2000) made ES a coherent, convex, LP-solvable objective, so you can run mean-CVaR optimization in place of mean-variance and read off an ES-implied required return: the price of tail risk times BTC's marginal contribution to portfolio ES. The key inputs are the fitted left tail (EVT/GPD, Hill tail index ~2.1-2.5, ES/VaR ratio) and the price-of-tail-risk the allocator charges. Because BTC's ES is enormous and left-skewed, the hurdle it must clear to be a fair "tail-insurance" position is far higher than variance-pricing implies. For a 10-15yr BTC CMA this argues two things: the appreciation needed to justify holding BTC on an ES-adjusted basis is steep, and the expected return you should pencil in is haircut downward because a large slice of BTC's raw return is compensation consumed by its tail. Borri (2019) adds that BTC's tail risk is intra-crypto, not shared with equities or gold.


*Scores — rigor 4, signal 2, robustness 3, data-ops 2, orthogonality 4. Methodologically strong: ES is a coherent, convex, LP-optimizable measure that correctly charges BTC for its documented heavy left tail (Rockafellar-Uryasev, EVT/GPD), fixing variance's symmetry — hence high rigor. But it is a normative hurdle engine, not a forecast: it tells you what BTC must return, not what it will, so its direct CMA-level signal over 10-15yr is weak and still requires an imported drift. The price-of-tail-risk is a free, unanchored parameter and ES estimation is fragile on BTC's short, bull-dominated history, hurting data_ops; robustness is middling since the tail/skew framing survives regime shifts better than cycle-timing methods but the multiplier and tail fit are unstable. Best used as a conservative skeptic's counter that conditions the downside, not as a standalone level.*


**Key drivers:** Fitted left-tail shape: EVT/GPD shape parameter and Hill tail index (BTC ~2.1-2.5, heavier than equities' ~3), driving the size of Expected Shortfall; ES/VaR ratio (BTC's far exceeds the Gaussian ~1.25), the single number that makes ES-pricing demand a higher hurdle than VaR- or variance-pricing; Price of tail risk / tail-risk aversion coefficient — the premium per unit of marginal ES the allocator charges (the Lagrange multiplier on the CVaR constraint); Marginal/component ES contribution of BTC to the total portfolio (Rockafellar-Uryasev decomposition; Marginal Expected Shortfall); Confidence level alpha (95% vs 99% vs 99.5%) — deeper tails raise the implied hurdle sharply for a fat-tailed asset; Tail dependence / tail-correlation with the rest of the portfolio (Borri CoVaR: BTC tail risk is intra-crypto, NOT shared with US equities or gold — so its marginal ES is largely idiosyncratic); Left-skewness and co-jump structure (correlated price-and-vol crashes) that fatten ES beyond what symmetric vol captures; Whether institutionalization/ETFs are compressing the tail forward (lower ES) or not


**Pros:** Uses a COHERENT, convex risk measure (Rockafellar-Uryasev): ES satisfies subadditivity and is LP-optimizable, fixing VaR's non-coherence and variance's symmetry — it charges BTC for its left tail specifically, which is the risk that actually matters for a crash-prone asset; Empirically disciplined on the tail it prices: fits BTC's documented heavy left tail (tail index ~2.1-2.5, ES >> VaR) with EVT/GPD rather than assuming Gaussian, so it does not understate the cost of holding BTC the way variance-pricing does; Produces a genuinely MORE CONSERVATIVE, higher hurdle than #15's variance-pricing — the correct direction for an asset whose ES dwarfs its VaR, making it a useful skeptic's counterweight to bullish CMAs; Has real empirical backing that downside/tail risk is PRICED in crypto: Zhang-Li (2021) find a positive, statistically significant downside-risk premium in the cross-section of ~2000 coins, validating the premise that ES contribution should earn compensation; Borri (2019) supplies a portfolio-relevant nuance the digital-gold camp ignores: BTC's tail risk is intra-crypto and NOT co-tail with equities or gold, so its marginal ES in a diversified book is partly idiosyncratic — a real, measurable input rather than a narrative; Convexity gives speedy, stable optimization (Man Group), so the implied hurdle is computable and refreshable from realized data, satisfying scripted-analysis discipline


**Cons:** It is a NORMATIVE/required-return engine, not a forecast: it tells you the return BTC MUST offer to be fairly priced as tail insurance, not the return it WILL deliver. Converting the hurdle into an expected-appreciation CMA still requires importing a drift from elsewhere (decay/adoption/TAM rows) — on its own it yields a hurdle, not a forecast; The price of tail risk (tail-aversion coefficient / Lagrange multiplier) is a free parameter with no market-observable anchor for BTC; the entire hurdle scales with it, so the 'required return' is as much a statement of the analyst's risk appetite as of BTC's risk; ES estimation is fragile on BTC's short, bull-dominated, ~13-16yr history with only ~4 cycles: the deep-tail (99/99.5%) ES and the GPD shape parameter are estimated off a handful of extremes, so standard errors are large and the implied hurdle is unstable across windows (Man Group: ES 'requires substantial historical data'); Backward-looking tail risk likely OVERSTATES forward ES if ETF/institutional access is genuinely compressing the leverage-feedback crashes that produced -77% to -93% drawdowns — yet there is too little post-institutional data to recalibrate, so the hurdle may be set too high; Pricing BTC purely on its OWN ES ignores that Borri's finding (tail-independence from equities and gold) makes BTC's marginal portfolio ES smaller than its standalone ES — a naive standalone-ES hurdle double-counts diversifiable tail risk and is too punitive; Says nothing native about cross-asset correlations beyond tail-dependence, and nothing about the right tail / convex upside — by construction it prices only the left tail, so it systematically understates the case for a convex, lottery-like asset and must be paired with an upside model; ES 'does little to protect against long, slow drawdowns' (Man Group) and is alpha-level-sensitive: the hurdle jumps discontinuously with the chosen confidence level, inviting cherry-picking

METHODOLOGY. The approach swaps the risk axis of the CMA from variance to a coherent downside measure, then turns that measure into a portfolio-implied required return. Rockafellar & Uryasev (2000, J. Risk 2:21-42) is the load-bearing reference: they showed Conditional Value-at-Risk — the expected loss conditional on being in the worst alpha-tail — is convex, coherent (subadditive, so diversification always helps), and minimizable as a linear program by introducing the auxiliary VaR variable and optimizing CVaR and VaR jointly. That tractability is what lets you replace mean-variance with mean-CVaR optimization. The required-return reading comes from the Lagrangian on the ES constraint: at the optimum, BTC's required excess return = (price of tail risk) x (BTC's marginal/component contribution to portfolio ES). Equivalently, the Euler allocation of ES gives each asset's tail 'cost'; an asset is fairly held only if its excess return clears that cost. Pricing BTC this way is pricing it as if you were WRITING tail insurance on it — you demand a premium proportional to the left-tail loss you are absorbing.

KEY RELATIONSHIPS. The reason this matters for BTC specifically is the ES/VaR gap. For a Gaussian, 95% ES/VaR ~ 1.25. BTC's return distribution is heavy-tailed and left-skewed: EVT/GPD fits and Hill-estimator studies put BTC's tail index alpha around 2.1-2.5 (vs ~3 for equities), so its ES sits far above its VaR and far above what a lognormal-with-60%-vol model implies. Mechanically, the heavier the tail, the larger the marginal ES, and the higher the ES-implied hurdle — which is exactly why this row demands a MORE conservative required return than #15's symmetric variance-pricing. Borri (2019, J. Empirical Finance 50:1-19) supplies the portfolio nuance via CoVaR: Bitcoin, Ether, Ripple and Litecoin are HIGHLY exposed to tail risk WITHIN crypto, but are NOT significantly exposed to the tail risk of the US equity market or gold. Two consequences for the CMA: (1) BTC's marginal portfolio ES is largely idiosyncratic, so a standalone-ES hurdle over-penalizes it (its tail does not co-arrive with the rest of a diversified book — at least in Borri's pre-2021 sample); and (2) on a tail-co-dependence basis BTC and gold are independent, which is the cleanest evidence in the entire study set AGAINST the digital-gold thesis — a true safe-haven substitute for gold would share gold's crash tail, and BTC does not.

HISTORICAL FIT / EMPIRICAL SUPPORT. The premise that downside/tail risk should command a premium is not merely assumed — Zhang & Li (2021, J. Banking & Finance 133) test it directly: across ~2000 cryptocurrencies, higher downside-risk (downside-beta) exposure is associated with significantly higher average returns, and the extra downside risk is priced with a statistically significant positive premium, while ordinary market risk is often insignificant. That is direct cross-sectional evidence that an ES/downside-risk hurdle is the right pricing axis for crypto. Man Group's 'Covering Your Tail' (2024) corroborates the practitioner case: two portfolios with identical variance and mean can have very different CVaR (their example: CVaR-0.4 of -1.32% vs -1.78%, the ES-optimized one ~25% better on worst days), ES's convexity gives speedy optimization, and it 'better targets extreme loss' than variance — but it 'requires substantial historical data' and 'does little to protect against long, slow drawdowns.'

FAILURE MODES. (1) It is normative, not predictive: it yields a hurdle, not an appreciation forecast, so a drift must still be imported — the row's contribution is the conservative SHADING of expected return, not the drift itself. (2) The price-of-tail-risk is a free parameter; the whole hurdle scales with the analyst's tail-aversion, with no BTC-observable anchor. (3) ES of a ~13-16yr, bull-dominated, 4-cycle series is estimated off a handful of extremes — deep-tail (99/99.5%) ES and GPD shape parameters have large standard errors and swing across windows. (4) If ETFs/institutionalization are genuinely compressing the leverage-feedback crash tail (the -77% to -93% historical drawdowns), backward-looking ES OVERstates forward tail cost and sets the hurdle too high — but there is too little post-institutional data to recalibrate. (5) Borri's tail-independence is pre-2021; ordinary BTC-equity correlation has since risen, and left-tail co-movement with growth equities now spikes in joint deleveraging, so the diversification credit ES-pricing extends to BTC is shrinking. (6) Pricing only the left tail systematically understates a convex, lottery-like asset — this row must be paired with a right-tail/upside model or it is structurally too bearish.

ON-RECORD MULTI-YEAR FORECASTS. There are no published 10-15yr BTC appreciation forecasts produced by this method — by construction it outputs hurdles and tail measures, not CMAs. The closest on-record artifacts are: Rockafellar-Uryasev's mean-CVaR optimization framework (the engine, asset-agnostic); Borri's CoVaR estimates that BTC tail risk is intra-crypto and tail-independent of equities and gold; Zhang-Li's significant positive downside-risk premium in the crypto cross-section; and the EVT/GPD studies that quantify BTC's ES >> VaR with tail index ~2.1-2.5. My synthesized CMA (~6-10% nominal / ~3-7% real, the most conservative of the return-process family) is my reconstruction of what an ES-aware allocator would pencil in after haircutting the decayed drift for BTC's outsized, idiosyncratic, gold-independent left tail — not a number any of these sources publish.

### #11 · Survival / Ruin-Probability (Absorbing-Zero Hazard)

*Family: survival-hazard · Source: Academia · Tier: Conditioning overlay · Overall 61*


**Explanation:** This approach treats Bitcoin's CMA as a probability-weighted mixture of two paths rather than a single number: E[R] = S(T)·R_survival + (1−S(T))·(−100%), where S(T)=exp(−∫h(t)dt) is cumulative survival under an annual ruin hazard h. It is the rigorous version of the 'left-tail haircut' other rows wave at. The inputs are: a hazard rate (a prior, ~1-3%/yr, possibly Lindy-declining per Ord 2023, since 16+ years and ETF adoption raise S(T)); a survival-path return R_survival borrowed from an adoption/TAM/decay model (~10-12%/yr); and a −100% recovery on the death path. Peer-reviewed theory supplies WHY a real zero-equilibrium exists — Schilling-Uhlig (JME 2019) collapse martingales and Biais et al. (J. Finance 2023) sunspot multiple-equilibria — while Taleb (2021) gives the absorbing-barrier intuition. For a 10-15yr BTC CMA it yields a bimodal payoff: ~80% mass on a right-skewed survival path, ~20% at −100%, centering the mean near ~7% nominal but making the mean itself a poor summary. Its value is shape and discipline, not a point estimate; it needs a survival-return model bolted on and says nothing about correlations or volatility.


*Scores — rigor 4, signal 2, robustness 4, data-ops 2, orthogonality 4. Theoretically clean: it makes BTC's dominant feature — a genuine point-mass at -100% — an explicit, auditable hazard rather than a buried fudge, grounded in real collapse-equilibrium theory (rigor 4). But empirical signal is weak: the hazard is near-unfalsifiable (n=1, still alive), so it's pure prior, and it's only a wrapper that still needs a survival-path return model — it adds tail conditioning but no level forecast (signal 2). Robustness is strong because pricing an absorbing state is regime-agnostic by construction — it doesn't depend on halving cycles, S2F, or correlation regimes (robustness 4). Data_ops is poor: the key parameter has no observable data to fit and the honest output is a distribution, not a CMA-ingestible point estimate, making it operationally awkward (data_ops 2).*


**Key drivers:** Annual hazard rate h(t) of the absorbing-zero state — the probability per year that the network is permanently abandoned / loses monetary value irreversibly (Fidelity's published anchor: ~0.71%/yr; practitioner ranges 1-5%/yr early, lower later); Hazard term-structure / Lindy decay: whether h(t) is constant, or declines with network age as security budget, liquidity, regulatory acceptance and adoption accrue (Ord 2023 mixture-of-exponentials => declining observed hazard => remaining-life ∝ current age); Cumulative survival probability S(T) = exp(-∫h(t)dt) over the 10-15yr horizon — the weight on the survival path; with h≈1%/yr and 12yr, S≈0.89; with h≈3%/yr, S≈0.70; Survival-path conditional return R_survival — the appreciation BTC earns CONDITIONAL on not dying (drawn from whichever fundamental model you trust: adoption S-curve, store-of-value TAM, monetary substitution); Recovery value on the death path (assumed -100%; some variants allow a small salvage/fork-residual, but the canonical absorbing state is zero and irreversible); Theoretical existence of the zero equilibrium: Schilling-Uhlig collapse supermartingale + Biais sunspot/multiple-equilibria coordination failure (the 'why' behind a non-zero hazard, independent of any technical exploit); Path-dependence / irreversibility (Taleb): once below a confidence/liquidity threshold the network's active-maintenance requirement makes zero an absorbing, non-recovering state — unlike gold whose value is not path-dependent


**Pros:** Honest about the dominant feature of BTC's payoff that almost every other CMA approach buries: a genuine, non-negligible point-mass at -100%. It turns the vague 'left-tail haircut' into an explicit, auditable parameter (the hazard) instead of a fudge factor.; Decomposable and modular: lets you bolt ANY survival-path return model (adoption S-curve, TAM, options-implied) onto a transparent ruin overlay, so the death risk is priced once, consistently, rather than smuggled into a lower point estimate.; Grounded in real, peer-reviewed theory for the EXISTENCE of the absorbing state — Schilling-Uhlig collapse equilibria and Biais et al. sunspots show zero can be a rational equilibrium with no exploit required, which is a far stronger argument than 'it might get hacked.'; Naturally produces the bimodal / heavily-right-skewed return distribution that matches BTC's empirical behavior, and makes the mean a poor summary statistic — pushing users toward median, mode, and probability-of-ruin, which is the correct mental model for position sizing.; The declining-hazard (Lindy) refinement is empirically motivated and testable: 16+ years of survival, growing institutional/ETF ownership and security budget are direct evidence that S(T) should be revised UP over time — the framework cleanly absorbs that evidence.; Mirrors how insurers, credit desks and venture portfolios already think (default/ruin probability * loss-given-default), so it ports a mature, well-understood risk discipline onto a new asset.


**Cons:** The hazard rate is essentially UNFALSIFIABLE over the horizons that matter: a 1%/yr vs 3%/yr vs 5%/yr 'death probability' swings the CMA enormously, yet there is one observed history (n=1, still alive) so the parameter is almost pure prior. Fidelity's 0.71% is a model output dressed as a measurement.; It only relocates the hard problem — you STILL need a survival-path return model, so survival-hazard is a wrapper, not a standalone valuation. Garbage R_survival in, garbage CMA out; the overlay can lend false rigor to a weak core forecast.; Taleb's strong form (any positive absorbing probability over infinite horizon => present value zero) is mathematically clean but economically self-undermining: it would also zero out any fiat currency, any single company, arguably any asset, since all have some irreversible-ruin probability over infinite time. The result hinges on infinite-horizon and a non-dividend assumption that real 10-15yr CMAs don't use.; Declining-hazard (Lindy) and the absorbing-barrier camp reach OPPOSITE conclusions from the same survival data, and the framework can't adjudicate — it just exposes the prior. Lindy assumes heterogeneity in a fixed unknown hazard; if BTC's hazard is genuinely time-varying or regime-dependent, the Pareto/Lindy scaling is unjustified.; Empirically thin estimation: the one peer-reviewed hazard study (Balutel & Voia 2023, Cox PH) models price-SHOCK timing, not network EXTINCTION — there is no clean event-history dataset of comparable-asset 'deaths' to fit a real baseline hazard to. The actuarial machinery is borrowed without the actuarial data.; Says NOTHING about correlations, volatility term structure, or cross-asset moments — it is purely a mean/ruin-of-the-distribution tool. Every co-movement figure a CMA needs must come from elsewhere, so as a CMA row it is structurally incomplete.; Behavioral mis-anchoring risk: a single published 'extinction probability' invites spurious precision and false comfort (or false alarm); the true uncertainty is on the hazard ITSELF, a second-order parameter the headline number hides.

METHODOLOGY. The CMA is a two-state mixture: E[R(T)] = S(T)*R_survival + (1-S(T))*(-100%), with S(T)=exp(-∫₀ᵀ h(t)dt). h(t) is the instantaneous annual hazard of entering an irreversible, absorbing zero. Everything turns on (a) the LEVEL of h and (b) its TERM STRUCTURE.\n\nWHY A ZERO STATE EXISTS (the genuinely academic part). Three independent arguments, none requiring a technical exploit: (1) SCHILLING-UHLIG, 'Some Simple Bitcoin Economics,' JME 106 (2019) 16-26 (NBER w24483; SSRN 3155310). In their endowment economy with Dollar and Bitcoin, the fundamental pricing equation makes the BTC/USD price a martingale in the simple case; under their conditions Bitcoin prices form convergent SUPERMARTINGALES that can drift to the fundamental value of zero — collapse is a rational equilibrium, a generalization of the Kareken-Wallace (1981) exchange-rate-indeterminacy result. (2) BIAIS, BISIÈRE, BOUVARD, CASAMATTA, MENKVELD, 'Equilibrium Bitcoin Pricing,' Journal of Finance 78(2), 2023, 967-1014 (DOI 10.1111/jofi.13206). Because current value depends on FUTURE transactional benefits which depend on future prices, the equation is self-referential => MULTIPLE EQUILIBRIA + SUNSPOTS => 'extrinsic volatility... prices fluctuate even when fundamentals are constant,' and a LARGER share of return variance is extrinsic than fundamental. A coordination shift can move agents off the positive-value equilibrium — i.e. a non-technical route to (near-)zero. (3) TALEB, 'Bitcoin, Currencies, and Fragility,' arXiv 2106.14204 (2021). Absorbing-barrier theorem: for a non-dividend asset, if there is ANY positive probability per period of hitting an irreversible zero, the present value over an infinite horizon is pulled to zero; BTC's reliance on continuous active maintenance makes zero absorbing and PATH-DEPENDENT, whereas gold's value is not path-dependent. This is the strong-form bound; I treat it as the left edge of the prior, not the central estimate, because the infinite-horizon + zero-recovery assumptions are inappropriate for a finite 10-15yr CMA.\n\nESTIMATING THE HAZARD. (a) FIDELITY's risk team publishes the cleanest usable number: a ~0.71%/yr Bitcoin 'extinction' probability from a 27-variable Monte Carlo, explicitly benchmarked against single-name equities (Tesla ~2.2%/yr, Apple ~0.06%/yr) — i.e. Fidelity literally treats network-death as a survivable-firm-style ruin probability. (b) BALUTEL & VOIA, 'Surviving the Storm: Hazard Models and Signaling Shocks in Bitcoin Prices,' Revue française d'économie XXXVIII (2023) 21-46, fit a COX PROPORTIONAL-HAZARD model — the canonical survival-analysis estimator — but to price-SHOCK timing, not extinction; it demonstrates the machinery is applicable to BTC while underscoring that no clean network-DEATH event-history dataset exists. (c) The DECLINING-hazard refinement: practitioners invoke the LINDY EFFECT (Bitcoin has outlived 450+ 'obituaries' since 2013), formalized by TOBY ORD, 'The Lindy Effect,' arXiv 2308.09045 (2023): if the true constant hazard is UNKNOWN and you mix exponential survival curves over a prior on that hazard, the observed/effective hazard DECLINES with age and remaining life expectancy scales with current age (Pareto tail). Implication for the CMA: S(T) should be revised UP as the network ages, so a constant-hazard model UNDER-states survival. The counter-camp (Mark Liu, 'Debunking the Lindy Effect for Cryptocurrencies') notes Lindy requires the right heterogeneity assumption and need not hold if BTC's hazard is genuinely regime-dependent.\n\nPRACTITIONER EV FORM. Bitcoin Magazine's 'Exploring Bitcoin Valuation Models' is the cleanest retail statement of the mixture: a five-outcome, arbitrarily-weighted distribution with an explicit zero outcome whose probability SHRINKS 'with each day that the Bitcoin network survives' while right-skew is preserved; their illustrative expected value was ~$150k/BTC. VanEck's Bitcoin LTCMA work is the asset-manager cousin (scenario-weighted price paths), though its headline is a TAM/adoption survival path rather than a formal hazard.\n\nWHY THE SHAPE BEATS THE POINT. The whole value of this row is that it refuses to collapse BTC to a single number. The payoff is BIMODAL: a fat point-mass at -100% plus a right-skewed survival lobe. Consequences a CMA user must respect: (i) the MEAN is a poor summary — median and mode of the survival lobe are much higher than the ruin-weighted mean, while the modal experience of a SINGLE investor is closer to the survival path OR total loss, rarely the mean; (ii) VOLATILITY is structurally elevated and does NOT decay to a survival-only floor because the absorbing mass fattens dispersion (this is why I synthesize ~65% vol vs the ~50% a survival-only model would print, and above the ~57% trailing-5y realized floor); (iii) position sizing should be driven by probability-of-ruin and Kelly/CVaR logic, not by E[R]. \n\nRELATION TO OTHER ROWS. This is the rigorous parent of every 'left-tail haircut' applied elsewhere (store-of-value TAM, adoption S-curve, options-implied): those rows lower a point estimate by a vague amount; this row makes the haircut an explicit, parameterized hazard and shows the haircut is not a translation of the mean but a CHANGE OF SHAPE. It is the natural complement to the Equilibrium/Game-Theoretic row (same Schilling-Uhlig/Biais theory) — that row explains WHY the zero equilibrium exists; this row PRICES the probability of reaching it.\n\nHONEST BOTTOM LINE. The hazard parameter is near-unfalsifiable (n=1, still alive), so the headline ~7% CMA is a thin veneer over a prior; the durable contribution is the SHAPE (bimodal, ~80% survival / ~19% ruin, vol ~65%) and the discipline of pricing ruin explicitly rather than smuggling it into a lower mean. Correlations are entirely judgment — the family produces no cross-asset moments — and gold correlation is kept ~0 because Taleb's own logic severs the digital-gold analogy.

### #12 · Bayesian Model-Averaging / Dynamic Model Averaging under Model & Parameter Instability

*Family: model-averaging · Source: Academia · Tier: Conditioning overlay · Overall 61*


**Explanation:** BMA/DMA is the ensemble layer that sits ON TOP of the other valuation lenses. Instead of betting on one model (S2F, Metcalfe, M2-elasticity, gold-TAM), it runs many candidate predictive models in parallel and weights each by its recent forecast performance, with forgetting factors that let both the weights and the regression coefficients drift over time. Two things move: which model is "best" (model uncertainty) and what its coefficients are (parameter instability). The deliverable is a combined predictive density — a central forecast plus genuinely wide intervals that widen when the models disagree. The signature academic finding (Catania-Grassi-Ravazzolo 2019; Bianchi-Guidolin-Pedio 2023) is that the optimal predictor set ROTATES across regimes and parameters are highly unstable, which directly justifies blending many lenses rather than committing to one. For a 10-15yr BTC CMA the honest implication is humbling: DMA/BMA produces no long-horizon edge — its predictability is short-horizon (≤180 days) and concentrated in investor attention, with stock factors, gold, and supply metrics NOT systematic predictors. It argues for a wide-interval, probability-weighted central case, not a precise number.


*Scores — rigor 5, signal 2, robustness 4, data-ops 2, orthogonality 4. Epistemically the most correct framing in the literature (peer-reviewed, explicitly models model+parameter instability and produces honest fat-tailed densities), so rigor and regime-robustness are high. But it yields NO native 10-15yr expected return — every crypto DMA/BMA application is sub-180-day and decays to near-zero, so its standalone signal for a decade-ahead level is weak. Operationally it is a heavy recursive ensemble requiring a maintained candidate set and refitting, not a drop-in CMA input, so data_ops is low. Its real value is conditioning/tails on top of the other lenses, not the level forecast the CMA needs.*


**Key drivers:** Model-probability weights: each candidate model weighted by its recursive predictive likelihood (posterior model probability), updated every period; Forgetting factors (alpha for model weights, lambda for coefficients): control how fast the ensemble discards stale models/parameters — the knobs that operationalize 'instability'; Time-varying coefficients (TVP): regression betas drift, so a predictor's loading can switch sign/magnitude across regimes (Bianchi-Guidolin-Pedio: SMB mean slope ~0.043 but unstable); The candidate predictor set itself: in the crypto applications ~17 predictors spanning market risk factors (SMB, equity), crypto-specific (volume, realized vol, hashrate/supply), sentiment/attention (Google search), gold spot, FX, VIX; Investor attention / search interest: the empirically DOMINANT time-varying predictor in the academic results, the one whose inclusion probability stays elevated; Predictive-interval width: a direct function of cross-model disagreement — the epistemic output that distinguishes this approach; Horizon: predictability concentrated at 1-day to ~180-day; effects decay to near-zero beyond ~180 days (a hard constraint on any long-horizon use)


**Pros:** Correct epistemics for a rotating-driver asset: explicitly models model uncertainty AND parameter instability instead of falsely committing to one lens — its own headline result (optimal predictor set is time-varying) is the strongest single justification in the literature for blending the 20 other approaches rather than picking one; Produces honest, wide predictive intervals: the combined density widens precisely when candidate models disagree, which is the right risk representation for BTC's fat-tailed, regime-shifting return distribution — and a built-in antidote to the false precision of S2F/Metcalfe/power-law point targets; Peer-reviewed and falsifiable: Catania-Grassi-Ravazzolo (Int. J. Forecasting), Bianchi-Guidolin-Pedio (Eur. J. Finance), Xiao-Sun (JRFM) use standard out-of-sample point/density scoring (log scores, directional accuracy, MCS) — real statistical machinery, not curve-fitting a price level; Empirically beats single models and naive benchmarks out-of-sample at short horizons (statistically significant point-forecast gains from univariate combinations; density gains from multivariate selection), and combinations support profitable directional strategies — genuine, if modest, predictive content; Disciplines hype: by letting weights flow to whichever model is currently forecasting well, it automatically down-weights a lens (e.g. S2F) when it breaks down, rather than locking in a discredited prior; Naturally accommodates appreciation DECAY and regime change because nothing is held constant — coefficients and model identity both adapt


**Cons:** Produces NO long-horizon expected return. Every academic DMA/BMA crypto application is short-horizon (1-day to ~180-day); effects decay to near-zero beyond ~180 days. Using it for a 10-15yr CMA is a category error — the method is a tactical, recursive forecaster, not a structural valuation model. It can discipline the OTHER lenses but cannot itself output a decade-ahead appreciation number.; Garbage-in still applies: BMA/DMA averages over a fixed CANDIDATE SET. If every candidate is a short-horizon, spurious-cointegration cousin (S2F, naive Metcalfe), averaging them yields a well-calibrated average of bad models — the ensemble cannot manufacture a structural anchor none of its members possess; The signature finding is deflationary for fundamental CMA: Bianchi-Guidolin-Pedio find crypto is NOT systematically predicted by stock-market factors, precious-metal commodities (gold), or supply factors — only by time-varying investor attention. This UNDERCUTS the gold-TAM/digital-gold and scarcity/supply lenses the CMA committee might want to lean on, and locates the only edge in a behavioral, non-fundamental, non-persistent driver; Forgetting-factor and prior choices are tuning knobs that materially move results; the method has many researcher degrees of freedom, and the short, bull-dominated sample (2014-2021) limits how stable the estimated instability itself is; Silent on cross-asset correlations and volatility magnitude as direct outputs — it forecasts the return series; the covariance vector vs equities/FI/TIPS/gold must be imported from realized data or another framework; Computationally and interpretively heavy relative to its modest, short-horizon payoff; 'the model changes every period' is honest but offers a portfolio committee little to anchor a 10-15yr assumption on

<details><summary>Full notes</summary>

WHAT IT IS. Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) and its dynamic cousin Dynamic Model Averaging (DMA, Raftery et al. 2010) are META-methods for forecasting under uncertainty about WHICH model is right and about WHETHER its coefficients are stable. You specify a bank of candidate predictive models (in crypto applications, dynamic linear / TVP regressions and VARs on a predictor set), and each period you weight each model by its recursive predictive likelihood. Two forgetting factors govern adaptivity: alpha discounts stale model weights, lambda discounts stale coefficient information. The output is a combined predictive DENSITY — a point forecast plus intervals that mechanically widen when the constituent models disagree. This is the right epistemic object for an asset whose drivers demonstrably rotate.

THE THREE CANONICAL SOURCES. (1) Catania, Grassi & Ravazzolo (2019, Int. J. Forecasting 35(2):485-501) apply DMA over a large set of univariate dynamic linear models and multivariate VARs with time variation to BTC, LTC, XRP, ETH. Headline: 'parameter instability is high and model preferences change over time' across all four coins; static models forecast poorly. They document statistically significant out-of-sample POINT gains from univariate combinations, DENSITY gains from multivariate selection, and 'sizable directional predictability' enough to support profitable strategies. (2) Bianchi, Guidolin & Pedio (2023, Eur. J. Finance 29(6):583-611; SSRN 3609949) run DMA with time-varying coefficients over 17 predictors spanning market risk factors (SMB, equity), crypto-specific variables, sentiment/attention, gold spot, and FX. Their decisive result: crypto returns are NOT systematically predicted by stock-market factors, precious-metal commodities, or supply factors — only by a 'time-varying but significant exposure to investors' attention.' Of 17 predictors, only a handful (~6) have 90% DMA-coefficient bands excluding zero; SMB's mean slope is ~0.043 but unstable. (3) Xiao & Sun (2020, JRFM 13(11):278) use shrinkage Mallows model averaging (SMMA) on an ARDL set and find crypto returns sensitive to financial-market volatility, gold prices, and FX, with SMMA beating penalized single-model estimators out-of-sample.

HISTORICAL FIT & FAILURE MODES. The method fits the data's CHARACTER honestly — it is built to detect instability and it finds plenty. But three caveats gut its use as a CMA engine. First, HORIZON: every application is short (1-day to ~180-day); a related Bayesian-local-projection result finds predictor effects largely vanish beyond ~180 days. There is simply no academic DMA/BMA BTC return forecast at a 10-15yr horizon — extrapolating one would be fabrication. Second, GARBAGE-IN: BMA averages over a fixed candidate set; if all members are short-horizon spurious-cointegration cousins, the average is a well-calibrated average of weak models. The method down-weights a broken lens (it would have shed S2F post-2021) but cannot create a structural anchor none of its members hold. Third, the SIGNATURE FINDING is deflationary: the only robust edge is investor attention — a behavioral, non-fundamental, non-persistent driver — while gold, equity factors, and supply metrics rotate in and out. The two papers even CONFLICT on gold (Xiao-Sun: in-sample relevant; Bianchi-Guidolin-Pedio: not a systematic predictor), which is itself the model-instability verdict and a direct caution against leaning the CMA on a stable BTC-gold linkage.

ON-RECORD MULTI-YEAR FORECASTS PRODUCED THIS WAY. None. This is important and worth stating plainly: no BMA/DMA crypto study publishes a multi-year point appreciation, real return, or correlation matrix. The literature publishes out-of-sample log scores, directional-accuracy ratios, MCS-set membership, and Value-at-Risk density evaluations at daily-to-semiannual horizons. Any 10-15yr number attributed to 'the model-averaging approach' is necessarily a synthesis overlay, not a cited output — which is why every cited cell here is 'n/a (source silent).'

HOW IT SHOULD BE USED IN THE CMA. Not as a 21st competing point estimate, but as the AGGREGATION LAYER and the epistemic conscience for the other 20. Its empirical message — the optimal predictor set is time-varying — is the single strongest in-literature justification for blending lenses and for attaching WIDE predictive intervals to the BTC CMA rather than a false-precision point. My synthesized central case (~9-10% nominal, ~6.5% real, vol ~57%, gold corr ~0.05-0.10) is exactly that: a probability-weighted average of the disciplined-decay estimates of the credible structural lenses, with the broken bull models (S2F/power-law) down-weighted as DMA would shed them, and intervals deliberately wide (90% band roughly -10% to +30%/yr nominal) to honor the model disagreement the method exists to quantify. The correlations are imported from realized data because the framework is silent on them. The deepest honest takeaway: the right answer for BTC is not a number but a probability-weighted distribution with fat tails — and this approach is the only one in the set whose entire purpose is to say so.

</details>

### #13 · Equilibrium / Game-Theoretic Security-Utility Pricing

*Family: dcf-moneyness · Source: Academia · Tier: Conditioning overlay · Overall 60*


**Explanation:** This family prices Bitcoin as a self-referential equilibrium rather than a cashflow asset. Value equals the present value of net transactional benefits (Biais et al., Journal of Finance 2023), jointly with the price that induces enough mining hashrate to keep the chain secure against a 51% attack (Liang Chen's RESUNE model, arXiv 2025; Houy 2014; Alden). Because both transactional usefulness and security scale with price, today's value depends on expected future prices — a fixed point that admits multiple equilibria and 'sunspot' (extrinsic) volatility even with constant fundamentals. The defining empirical result is decompositional: a larger share of Bitcoin's return variance is extrinsic, not fundamental. These are positive models explaining price formation and high volatility, not forecasts — they publish no expected return. For a 10-15yr CMA that means no native point estimate; the honest takeaways are perpetual elevated volatility (~55-70%, uniquely model-implied here, not just borrowed) and a fee-market terminal-security risk that Houy shows may not even guarantee long-run viability. Appreciation must be imported as judgment (~8-10% nominal).


*Scores — rigor 5, signal 2, robustness 4, data-ops 2, orthogonality 4. Theoretical ceiling of the BTC-valuation families: peer-reviewed (JF 2023), microfounded, fixed-point value from transactional benefit + security budget — hence rigor 5. But it explicitly declines to forecast; multiple-equilibria/sunspot results make it consistent with almost any path, so signal and data_ops are weak (no point return, vol, or correlation output; synthesized 8-10% is admitted judgment). Robustness is its real strength (4): never relied on S2F/halving regularities, so it survives the 2021 break and ETF-era correlation shift, docked only for the unsolved fee-funded-security terminal state.*


**Key drivers:** Net transactional benefits: the flow utility of holding/using BTC for transactions and store-of-value, indexed empirically (Biais et al.); Self-referential fixed point: fundamental value depends on future prices, generating multiple equilibria and sunspot (extrinsic) volatility even with constant fundamentals; Security budget = block subsidy + transaction fees; must remain large enough that cost-to-attack > attack payoff (Chen, Houy, Alden); Endogenous hashrate via free-entry zero-profit miner condition: F^-1(H) = P*(B+Phi)/H; Halving dynamics: as block subsidy B -> 0, security must be carried by fees Phi; viability of the fee market is the central open question; Attack-cost / security-utility coupling: higher price -> larger security budget -> more attack resistance -> supports demand (reflexive loop); Fixed supply Q clears against speculative + transactional demand D(P, security)


**Pros:** Genuinely peer-reviewed (Journal of Finance) and microfounded; derives value from first principles rather than curve-fitting, unlike S2F/Metcalfe; Honestly explains why BTC is so volatile: multiple equilibria + sunspots are a feature of the model, not noise to be assumed away; Provides a falsifiable lower-bound discipline — the chain is only worth holding if the fee-funded security budget can deter attack as subsidy decays, tying long-run value to real adoption/fee demand; Avoids the 'no cashflow so unvaluable' dead-end by identifying transactional-benefit and security streams as the economic substitute for cashflow; Comparative statics (halving lowers P and H together; fee market must develop) give a coherent narrative for the appreciation-decay path


**Cons:** Produces essentially NO usable point CMA: no closed-form steady-state price, no expected-return number, no volatility forecast, no correlation outputs — the papers explicitly decline to forecast; Multiple-equilibria / sunspot result means the model is consistent with almost any price path, which is intellectually honest but useless for a single 10-15yr expected return; The fee-based-security terminal state is unsolved: Chen, Houy and Alden all flag 'whether fee demand can fund security' as an OPEN question — the long-run equilibrium may not exist or may be fragile (tragedy-of-the-commons free-riding on security); Net-transactional-benefit indices are noisy proxies; calibration shows fundamentals explain only a minority of return variance, so the 'fundamental' anchor is weak; Reflexivity (price -> security -> value) makes the model prone to self-fulfilling collapse as well as boom; it does not pin down which equilibrium prevails; These academic models are frequently conflated in marketing with S2F/Metcalfe, which the literature largely REJECTS as spurious: S2F is a regression of two non-stationary series (spurious cointegration, serially correlated residuals) that broke decisively post-2021 (predicted ~$100k+ in 2022, BTC crashed); naive Metcalfe network-value fits are likewise overfit and non-robust. Do not let the rigorous equilibrium work launder the discredited scarcity/network curves.

<details><summary>Full notes</summary>

METHODOLOGY. Two distinct but related academic strands, plus practitioner work, share the 'value = transactional-benefit + security, not cashflow' premise.\n\n(1) Biais, Bisière, Bouvard, Casamatta & Menkveld, 'Equilibrium Bitcoin Pricing,' Journal of Finance 78(2), 2023, pp. 967-1014 (the seed DOI 10.1111/jofi.13119 in the prompt resolves to the published 10.1111/jofi.13206). General-equilibrium overlapping-generations-style model: 'The fundamental value of the cryptocurrency is its stream of net transactional benefits, which depend on its future prices.' Because current fundamentals depend on FUTURE prices, the pricing equation is self-referential -> multiple equilibria and SUNSPOTS -> 'extrinsic volatility, that is, cryptocurrency prices fluctuate even when fundamentals are constant.' They build empirical indices of net transactional benefits and calibrate; key qualitative result: 'part of the variations in Bitcoin returns reflects changes in net transactional benefits, but a LARGER share reflects extrinsic volatility.' This is the single most important, citable, peer-reviewed quantitative-flavored finding in the whole family — and it is a humility result, not a price target. No expected return, vol, or correlation numbers are published.\n\n(2) Liang Chen, 'A Game-Theoretic Foundation for Bitcoin's Price: A Security-Utility Equilibrium,' arXiv 2508.06071, 2024 (working paper, NOT peer-reviewed). Defines a 'Rational-Expectations Security-Utility Nash Equilibrium' (RESUNE). Market clears on fixed supply Q: D(P*, ς(P*,H(P*))) = Q (Eq.6), with free-entry miner zero-profit condition F^-1(H) = P*(B+Phi)/H (Eq.2), where B=block subsidy, Phi=fees, H=hashrate, ς=security via a global-games coordination model. NO closed-form price, NO steady-state appreciation/vol, only comparative statics (halving lowers P and H jointly) and a VAR for empirical testing. Explicitly: 'as B->0, miner revenue becomes entirely dependent on fees' and 'whether the demand for block space can generate such fees is a critical open question for Bitcoin's future.' So the terminal equilibrium is unsolved.\n\n(3) Nicolas Houy, 'The Economics of Bitcoin Transaction Fees,' SSRN 2014 — early game-theoretic treatment of the fee market and the zero/positive-fee equilibria; foundational for the security-budget strand (couldn't fetch full text, 403; cited from secondary summaries and its canonical role).\n\n(4) Lyn Alden, 'Bitcoin: Fee-Based Security Modeling' (practitioner, ~2021). Most concrete numbers, but practitioner not academic: argues long-run security spend should be ~0.5-1.5% of market cap/yr; 2020 snapshot ~2.5% of $203.5B cap, ~$5B miner revenue, ~$44 all-in cost/tx; frames the transition as 'middling risk.' Quotes Satoshi: 'in 20 years there will either be very large transaction volume or no volume.' No price target — binary framing: sufficient fee demand sustains security and value, or BTC fails the transition.\n\nBRUTAL HONESTY ON S2F/METCALFE. The prompt's mandate: this rigorous equilibrium work is routinely conflated in marketing with stock-to-flow and Metcalfe curves, which the academic/quant literature LARGELY REJECTS in naive form. S2F (PlanB) regresses two non-stationary I(1) series (price on stock/flow ratio) -> classic SPURIOUS regression; residuals are serially correlated; Engle-Granger/Johansen 'cointegration' claims do not survive proper specification (see Burger's multi-part review; Matt Paz 'Falsifying Stock-to-Flow'). The model fit 2015-2021 then BROKE: it implied ~$100k+ in 2022, BTC fell to ~$16k. Naive Metcalfe (value ∝ users^2 / active addresses^2) is an overfit, non-robust curve with no stationary error-correction. NONE of this belongs in a CMA except as a cautionary note; the equilibrium models above are the defensible version of 'fundamental' Bitcoin pricing and they pointedly do NOT produce the tidy exponential price targets the scarcity/network curves advertise.\n\nWHY THE CMA IS A JUDGMENT, NOT A MODEL OUTPUT. The family is positive, not normative — it explains volatility and price formation, declines to forecast. My synthesized_outputs are MY extrapolation under the family's logic, anchored to the prompt's realized-decay baseline (142->65->17 %/yr). Scripted extrapolation (decaying the growth RATE ~10%/yr with a ~7% mature-risk-asset floor over 15yr) yields ~9% nominal average, ~7% terminal, ~6.5% real — I report ~8-10% nominal / ~6-7% real. Vol stays high (~55-70%) precisely BECAUSE the model predicts persistent sunspot/extrinsic volatility and multiple equilibria. Correlations are weak/unstable: the demand side is speculative risk-on (gives modest + to growth equities, near-zero to fixed income, mild + to gold via the store-of-value/security framing). Critically, this family does NOT validate a tight BTC-gold correlation or an inflation-hedge property — value here is transactional-benefit + security, not a CPI or scarcity claim — so the 'digital gold' thesis gets only weak, qualified support (corr_gold ~+0.1 to +0.3). All correlation/vol numbers are reasoned judgments, flagged as such, since the source literature is silent.

### #14 · ML Realized-Volatility & Vol-Term-Structure Forecasting (HAR-RV / GARCH / Hybrid)

*Family: vol-forecasting · Source: Academia · Tier: Conditioning overlay · Overall 60*


**Explanation:** These models forecast Bitcoin's volatility, not its price. HAR-RV regresses tomorrow's realized vol on daily, weekly and monthly RV averages built from high-frequency returns; GARCH variants model conditional variance with a long-run mean it reverts toward; ML/LSTM-GARCH hybrids learn nonlinear vol dynamics, sometimes feeding GARCH outputs as features. The key inputs are high-frequency RV, a continuous-vs-jump decomposition, leverage asymmetry, and the mean-reversion speed that sets the term structure. For a 10-15yr BTC CMA the value is the volatility cell and its shape: you extrapolate the mean-reverting RV process beyond the ~6-month option-implied limit to a long-run unconditional sigma. The honest implication is a ~50-60% decade-average floor — vol mean-reverts and has trended down with ETF institutionalization (spot dipping toward ~40% in calm 2024-25 windows), but the models give no basis to forecast convergence to gold-like levels. They are silent on appreciation and correlation, so those must be imported.


*Scores — rigor 4, signal 2, robustness 3, data-ops 4, orthogonality 3. Methodologically sound for second moments (HAR-RV/GARCH are well-validated, parsimonious, with continuous/jump decomposition), earning high rigor. But signal for a 10-15yr CMA is weak: it is silent on appreciation and correlation by construction, and the 1-day-to-2-month validation horizon makes long-run sigma an out-of-model assertion, not a forecast — the decay anchor and correlation cells must be imported. Mean-reversion gives moderate regime robustness but it never saw a multi-cycle BTC equilibrium. Data (high-frequency RV) is abundant and the OLS/GARCH fit is operationally trivial, so data_ops is strong; net value to the CMA is narrow (the vol cell only).*


**Key drivers:** High-frequency realized variance/volatility (5-min returns) as the core observable, with the daily/weekly/monthly HAR cascade capturing long memory (heterogeneous market participants); Continuous (diffusive) vs jump decomposition (bipower variation, realized semivariances) — jumps are frequent in BTC and the jump term materially improves forecasts; separating them sets the diffusive 'floor'; Mean-reversion speed and the long-run unconditional variance (GARCH alpha+beta persistence; HAR component decay) that govern how fast vol reverts and thus the term-structure slope; Leverage/asymmetry (EGARCH/GJR; HAR with signed semivariance) — BTC shows a documented inverse/atypical leverage effect; Heavy-tailed, time-varying skew/kurtosis innovations (skewed-t, score-driven) — conventional Gaussian GARCH underperforms; Model class / estimation window choice (HAR vs GARCH vs LSTM-GARCH; rolling-window length) which can swamp the model-choice effect; Institutionalization/liquidity regime (ETF flows, deeper order books) as a slow structural driver lowering the unconditional vol level over the horizon


**Pros:** Produces the actual decade-horizon volatility number AND its mean-reverting term structure from data — the one CMA cell BTC's no-cashflow problem doesn't break — extending past the ~6-month liquid-option limit where the implied-vol (#11) approach runs out; Empirically validated and parsimonious: HAR-RV (Corsi 2009) reproduces long memory/fat tails/self-similarity with OLS and forecasts remarkably well; HAR-on-realized-variance beats daily-data GARCH, with the edge largest at short horizons; Separates continuous from jump volatility, so the 'floor' (diffusive vol) is identified apart from crash risk — directly useful for sizing and tail budgeting, and the jump term is statistically significant and improves accuracy; Honest about the floor: the literature's central message — that BTC vol mean-reverts to ~50-60%, not to gold-like levels — is exactly the discipline a credible BTC CMA needs against 'vol will converge to equities/gold' hype; ML/hybrid extensions (LSTM, CNN-LSTM) can beat GARCH out-of-sample at multiple horizons (Huang-Sangiorgi-Urquhart 2024) and ingest exogenous predictors (other cryptos, commodities, on-chain, uncertainty/sentiment)


**Cons:** Silent on appreciation and correlation by construction — it is a second-moment model only; the entire return/CMA-mean and every correlation cell must be borrowed from another framework, so it cannot stand alone as a CMA; Horizon mismatch is severe: these are 1-day to ~1-2-month forecasting models validated in-sample; extrapolating a mean-reverting RV/GARCH process to 10-15 years is an out-of-model assumption (you are really just asserting the long-run unconditional sigma), and adjusted-R2-best models differ across horizons; ML gains are fragile and often not statistically significant: the LSTM-GARCH paper (PMC10013303) found a plain MLP best with no DM-significant edge over LSTM/GARCH, on only 6 pandemic months; 'HARd to Beat' shows rolling-window choice can dominate the model choice — easy to overfit and over-claim; Regime/structural-break risk: vol is non-stationary and has fallen sharply with ETF institutionalization (toward ~40% in calm 2024-25 windows); a model fit on the volatile 2017-2022 era can mis-set the long-run floor in either direction, and the 21M-cap/leverage feedbacks producing jumps are not stable parameters; Conditional/short-horizon vol is not the unconditional decade vol: averaging a mean-reverting process over 10-15yr that includes 60-80% drawdown episodes yields a higher number than any tranquil-period nowcast, so naive use of a low current RV understates the CMA vol
